content.text: Unix originated in 1969 at AT&T's Bell Labs, where Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie, and others developed it as a successor to the Multics project. In the early 1970s, it was rewritten in the C programming language, making it remarkably portable across hardware platforms—a key factor in its widespread adoption. Throughout the 1980s, Unix branched into competing variants, most notably AT&T's System V and the Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) from UC Berkeley. Its design philosophy and core concepts went on to influence virtually every modern operating system, including Linux, macOS, and the broader POSIX ecosystem.
